content: Acute upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs), such as the common cold and rhinosinusitis, are widespread conditions that cause significant discomfort and functional impairment. These infections are a major contributor to workplace absenteeism. Treatment typically involves the use of antipyretic and decongestant medications, and occasionally antibiotics, despite the fact that most URTIs are caused by viral pathogens. Saline nasal irrigation is frequently used as an adjunctive therapy to alleviate URTI symptoms, although there is limited evidence supporting its efficacy in this context. This review updates a previous Cochrane review by Kassel et al., which suggested that saline irrigation might reduce the severity of certain symptoms associated with acute URTIs. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of saline nasal irrigation in managing the symptoms of acute URTIs. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, AMED, and LILACS, covering studies published up to August 2014. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared topical nasal saline treatments to other interventions in both adults and children diagnosed with acute URTIs. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the included trials using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool and extracted relevant data. Statistical analysis was performed using the Cochrane Review Manager software. However, due to significant variability in the outcome measures reported across studies, only a limited number of outcomes could be combined for statistical analysis. The review included five RCTs involving a total of 544 children (from three studies) and 205 adults (from two studies). These trials compared saline nasal irrigation to routine care or other nasal sprays, rather than to a placebo. Two new trials were added in this update, but their data were insufficient in size or quality to alter the original findings. Most of the included trials were small and of low quality, leading to an unclear risk of bias. The variability in outcome measures across studies further limited the ability to pool results. Overall, most studies found no significant difference between saline nasal irrigation and control treatments. However, one larger trial conducted in children demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in nasal secretion scores (mean difference [MD] -0.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.48 to -0.14) and nasal obstruction scores (MD -0.33, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.19) in the saline group. Despite these findings, the clinical significance of a mean difference of -0.33 on a four-point symptom scale is likely minimal. This trial also reported a significant reduction in the use of decongestant medications among participants in the saline group. Minor nasal discomfort or irritation was the only side effect reported, and it occurred in a small number of participants. In conclusion, saline nasal irrigation may offer some benefits in alleviating the symptoms of acute URTIs. However, the evidence is limited by the small size and low quality of the included trials, as well as the high risk of bias. These limitations reduce confidence in the findings. Future research should focus on conducting larger, high-quality trials with standardized and clinically meaningful outcome measures to better assess the efficacy of saline nasal irrigation in this context.
